More conservative estimates from IEA estimate global production and consumption around 150 MMT/yr by 2050 (IEA 2024b). Of the hydrogen produced in the United States at present, roughly 95% is from a mature production process called natural gas reforming (DOE n.d.-d). Hydrogen produced through this process is colloquially referred to as gray hydrogen. Notably, steam methane reforming (SMR) is the most common form of natural gas reforming seen in the United States. At a global scale, natural gas reforming remains the most prominent hydrogen production technology, accounting for roughly 60% of global hydrogen production. China also produces a significant amount of hydrogen through coal gasification (brown hydrogen), a process that accounts for about 20% of global production (IEA 2024a). Conventional fossil-based hydrogen production facilities (such reformers and gasifiers) typically operate near capacity, with shut-off only for scheduled maintenance. This is primarily due to the high temperature of production processes, which take time to reach operating conditions from a cold start. Figure 31 details the process flow diagram for an SMR facility. The primary hydrogen production steps occur within the reformer and water-gas shift (WGS) reactors. (2020) SMR with carbon capture and storage (SMR-CCS) and auto-thermal reforming with carbon capture and storage (ATR-CCS) are two other notable fossil-based hydrogen production 45 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. pathways gaining traction due to the low-pollution nature of the production process. Hydrogen produced via these two pathways is commonly called blue hydrogen. ATR is very similar to SMR in that both are natural gas reforming processes. The primary difference is that auto- thermal reformers are fed pure oxygen to provide heat for reaction (Figure 32), while steam methane reformers are heated externally, usually through natural gas combustion (Figure 31). It is expected that newly built ATR-CCS installations will outpace new SMR-CCS facilities due to the ease at which CO can be captured from the ATR hydrogen production process. SMR-CCS 2 facilities that are in operation today are typically not new facilities but are established SMR facilities that have been retrofitted with carbon capture technology to reduce process pollution (DOE n.d.-e). At an existing SMR plant, CO capture equipment can be installed either at the 2 flue gas stack or after the water-gas shift reactor. In the latter option, only process CO can be 2 captured (about 60% of total CO ), but the CO is at a higher pressure, making it easier and 2 2 lower cost to capture compared to capture at the flue gas stack (Antonini et al. 2020; Salais 2021; Bracci et al. 2022).
